planting.note: Plant rooted offshoots in spring in deep, well-drained oasis soil in full sun; Alligue needs the same long, hot, dry summer as other commercial dates to properly cure its fruit.

directions: Alligue, also sold under its Arabic name Ftimi, is Tunisia's second most widely grown date cultivar after Deglet Noor, concentrated in the Kebili and Gabes oases of the Djerid and Nefzaoua regions. It ripens earlier in the season than Deglet Noor and produces a softer, deep amber-to-brown fruit with moister flesh that is favored for immediate local consumption and traditional date paste rather than for long-distance export. Like other commercial dates it needs an extremely long, hot, arid growing season and irrigated oasis conditions to properly sweeten on the tree, and female palms require a nearby male palm or hand pollination to set fruit. Expect several years of establishment growth before young offshoots reach bearing age.
sources: FAO Date Palm Global Network cultivar records
Institut National de la Recherche Agronomique de Tunisie (INRAT)

planting.note: Plant grafted or rooted-cutting trees in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Chetoui sets fruit more reliably with a second olive cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Chetoui is the dominant olive cultivar of northern Tunisia's Beja and Mateur growing districts, prized for oil with a notably high polyphenol content and a pronounced bitter, pungent, grassy flavor that contrasts with the milder oil from Tunisia's more widely planted southern Chemlali cultivar. It tolerates the cooler, wetter winters of the Tell Atlas foothills better than drought-adapted southern cultivars, and growers there often rely on rainfall alone once trees are established rather than irrigating. Chetoui is only partially self-fertile and bears a more consistent crop when interplanted with a compatible cultivar, with fruit typically hand-harvested or lightly shaken from the tree in early winter for pressing. Give it full sun and well-drained soil, since it remains intolerant of waterlogging despite the wetter climate it is traditionally grown in.
sources: International Olive Council — World Catalogue of Olive Varieties

common_name: Oued Zenati Durum Wheat (Algerian Heirloom Semolina Wheat)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill seed in autumn across the eastern Algerian high plains where this landrace has long been grown as a rainfed winter cereal, letting plants establish before winter and resume growth with spring rains.

directions: Oued Zenati is a durum wheat landrace from the high plains around Guelma and Constantine in eastern Algeria, long valued by North African breeders as a source of drought and heat tolerance and used for generations as a parent line in Mediterranean durum improvement programs. Grown as a rainfed winter cereal, it is traditionally broadcast into tilled ground in autumn and left to overwinter on stored soil moisture, producing the hard, amber, high-protein grain prized across the Maghreb for rolling into couscous semolina and traditional flatbreads. It tends toward taller, more lodging-prone straw than modern semi-dwarf durums, so it performs best on lean soil without heavy nitrogen inputs. Harvest once heads are fully dry and golden, typically in early summer in its native growing region.
sources: ICARDA (International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas) durum wheat germplasm records
Institut National de la Recherche Agronomique d'Algérie (INRAA)

common_name: Imilla Negra Potato (Bolivian Highland Purple Potato)

planting.note: Plant seed tubers 3-4 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil once soil has warmed and hard frost danger has passed; Imilla Negra is traditionally grown at high Andean altitude under cool nights and intense sun.

directions: Imilla Negra is one of Bolivia's most recognizable native potatoes, named for its deep purple-black skin ('imilla,' meaning young woman in Quechua and Aymara, is a common prefix for Bolivian potato landraces) and sold fresh in La Paz and Cochabamba produce markets rather than grown for export. Smallholders cultivate it at high Andean altitude on terraced or sloped fields, where cool nights and intense highland sun concentrate its earthy flavor and dense, floury flesh. Hill the plants as they grow to keep developing tubers covered and prevent sun greening, and harvest once foliage dies back late in the season. It keeps reasonably well in the cool, dark conditions of traditional Andean root cellars.
sources: International Potato Center (CIP) — Andean potato landrace catalog

planting.note: Plant seed tubers in loose, well-drained soil at the start of the growing season; Waycha is a longer-season highland variety that needs more time to bulk tubers than quick-maturing lowland potatoes.

directions: Waycha is Bolivia's most widely planted native potato, grown across the Altiplano and high valleys from Potosí to La Paz by smallholders who value its reliable yields on poor, rocky, high-altitude soils. Its round, smooth-skinned, cream-colored tubers with pale yellow flesh are eaten fresh but are also among the preferred varieties for freeze-drying into chuño and tunta, traditional preserved potato staples made by alternating nighttime freezing with daytime sun exposure. Plant tubers in loose, well-drained soil and hill as plants grow, allowing for a notably longer season to bulk tubers than fast-maturing lowland potato varieties. Harvest after foliage dies back and cure tubers briefly in a shaded, airy spot before storage.
sources: International Potato Center (CIP) — Andean potato landrace catalog

common_name: Luk'i Bitter Potato (Bolivian Frost-Hardy High-Altitude Potato)

planting.note: Plant seed tubers in lean, well-drained high-altitude soil; Luk'i tolerates hard overnight frosts that kill common potato varieties, reflecting its origin as a hybrid with frost-resistant wild relatives.

directions: Luk'i belongs not to the common potato species but to Solanum juzepczukii, a distinct bitter potato grown by Aymara and Quechua farmers on Bolivia's high Altiplano at elevations where ordinary potatoes fail to survive. Its small tubers carry high levels of bitter glycoalkaloids that make them inedible fresh, so they are traditionally processed into chuño or tunta through repeated cycles of nighttime freezing, foot-trampling, and sun-drying that leach out the bitterness and yield a lightweight, long-storing staple. The species withstands hard overnight frosts that would kill common potato varieties outright, a legacy of its ancestry as a natural hybrid between cultivated potato and frost-resistant wild relatives. Grow it in lean, well-drained, high-altitude soil with minimal inputs, since it is adapted to marginal ground where little else produces a reliable crop.
sources: International Potato Center (CIP) — bitter potato (Solanum juzepczukii) germplasm records

common_name: Alto Beni Criollo Cacao (Bolivian Heirloom Fine-Flavor Cacao)

planting.note: Transplant into deep shade with warm, humid, wind-protected conditions well after all danger of cool weather has passed.

directions: Alto Beni Criollo refers to the native criollo-type cacao long cultivated by smallholder families in Bolivia's Alto Beni region northeast of La Paz, where cooperative-grown beans have built a reputation among chocolate makers for a mild, aromatic, low-bitterness flavor typical of criollo lineage. Trees are smaller and less vigorous than bulk-cacao hybrids and their pods are more vulnerable to fungal disease, so growers interplant them under taller shade trees in the diverse agroforestry systems traditional to the region. Give it constant warmth, high humidity, and dappled shade with excellent drainage, since criollo cacao has essentially no cold tolerance and dislikes waterlogged soil. Pods are hand-harvested as they ripen, then fermented and dried slowly to develop the fruity, floral notes prized in fine-flavor chocolate.
sources: Fine Cacao and Chocolate Institute — Bolivian cacao profiles
El Ceibo cooperative, Alto Beni, Bolivia

planting.note: Direct sow around the last frost date into well-drained soil in full sun; Tunkahuan grows taller and later-maturing than short-season breeding lines developed for temperate climates.

directions: Tunkahuan is a quinoa variety released by Ecuador's national agricultural research institute (INIAP) from highland landraces collected around Chimborazo and Carchi provinces, selected for a more uniform white seed and better resistance to downy mildew than unimproved local types. It grows considerably taller and later-maturing than dwarf breeding lines developed for high-latitude climates, reflecting its origin in equatorial highland valleys with long, mild growing seasons. Direct sow into well-drained soil in full sun and stake or interplant it with other tall crops in windy sites, since mature plants can lodge under their heavy seed heads. Harvest whole panicles once seed rattles and dries, then thresh and rinse thoroughly to strip the bitter saponin coating before cooking.
sources: INIAP (Instituto Nacional de Investigaciones Agropecuarias), Ecuador
FAO — Andean Grains: Amaranth, Quinoa and Kañiwa

common_name: INIAP Alegría Amaranth (Ecuadorian Highland Grain Amaranth)

planting.note: Direct sow into warm soil after all danger of frost has passed in full sun; thin seedlings as they establish since mature plants need room to bulk their seed heads.

directions: INIAP Alegría is a grain amaranth variety released by Ecuador's national agricultural research institute (INIAP) from Andean Amaranthus caudatus landraces gathered in the northern highland provinces of Imbabura and Cotopaxi. It was selected for more uniform ripening and a more compact, upright seed head than sprawling traditional landrace types, easing harvest and threshing for small producers. Toasted, popped grain from this variety is the signature ingredient in Ecuador's traditional alegría candy bars, bound with honey or panela syrup, which lent the variety its name. Direct sow into warm soil after frost danger has passed in full sun, and cut whole seed heads once they dry and rattle, then thresh and winnow to separate the tiny seed from chaff.
sources: INIAP (Instituto Nacional de Investigaciones Agropecuarias), Ecuador
FAO — Andean Grains: Amaranth, Quinoa and Kañiwa
